posts.content:
Last month, the Airtable Academy team transformed our entire operating system with a fleet of new agents and agentic workflows. This one helped us increase our publishing output by 125% while maintaining learner CSAT and improving our influenced product usage. Check it out👇

For those unfamiliar, Airtable Academy is the home for our customer education programs -- the self-paced courses, certifications, and learning experiences that help Airtable users of all kind (builders, enterprise admins, end-users) be more successful and effective in their work.

And as anyone in customer education knows, good, effective educational content is cross-functional and time-intensive. A single lesson could mean a script in Docs, graphics and visuals in Slides, a walkthrough-ready demo base with dummy data in Airtable, eLearning assets, knowledge checks, additional resources, etc. etc. etc. -- and that's *before* you pull in product SMEs for review, tap extra resources for video editing, or think about where the lesson fits in the wider catalog.

So the team built an agent that collapses all of it into a single Slack thread. Drop your topic in and get back the full bundle: script, deck, demo base, and a complete eLearning module with a quiz. 

With the skills we've built in, it draws on our learner feedback surveys, anchors to our existing catalog and our product roadmap (both stored in Airtable, obv), applies AEO best practices for LLM discoverability, and uses psychometric principles to build the quiz. 

And because our full tech stack has opened their MCPs, it drafts AND it publishes directly into our tools once the human-in-the-loop approves. Our process has become fully headless.

This past quarter, this agent allowed us to publish 125% more content than a normal sprint. Same team. Same time. Learner CSAT held at 8.9 on the new content, and product usage among course completers jumped +130% in the 30 days after.

This won the individual "Builder Prize" and helped us take home the "Team Breakthrough" prize during Airloop, Airtable's internal agent building competition. And now, it runs every day.

posts.content:
For the past few months, I've had an AI agent deliver a personalized AI briefing to my inbox every Friday. It pulls together the week's most important developments across foundation models & research, business & market moves, developer tools, enterprise AI adoption, policy & regulation, platform announcements, and a handful of other stories.

For each story, it provides a link to the full article/source, a TL;DR summary, and a note on why it's important/relevant.

I've found it helpful because AI news is happening *very* fast and it's increasingly fragmented -- important developments are spread across research labs, startups, big tech, regulators, and hundreds of newspapers, blogs, and social feeds.

I'm wondering if this would be valuable to others as well. Would there be any sort of appetite if I turned this into a public weekly newsletter?

Here are a few headlines from this week's briefing:

• Microsoft launched its first in-house AI model at Build 2026. MAI-Thinking-1 was trained without OpenAI data and reportedly matches Opus 4.6 on coding benchmarks.

• Anthropic submitted draft IPO paperwork to the SEC this week at a $965B valuation, targeting a fall 2026 NASDAQ listing that would rank among the largest U.S. tech debuts ever. $47 billion in annualized revenue, up from $9B at the end of last year, and driven primarily by coding agents.

• AI agents jumped from 12% to 66% task success in a single year per Stanford's AI Index. They're 6 points away from human-level on real computer tasks. The bottleneck now is governance, not capability.

• GitHub Copilot ended unlimited AI for developers. Usage-based billing is live as of June 1. The trigger? Multi-hour autonomous coding agent sessions are dramatically more compute-intensive than a quick chat, and GitHub has been quietly absorbing that escalating cost.

Let’s not bury the lede: Airtable Buildathon was insane. 

For an event we’d never run before, with two-ish months of lead time, I had an *immense* amount of conviction (maybe too much, if you ask my team) that it would work. And boy did it.

I remember in that first planning meeting, I kept waiting for someone to shut down (or at least question) the initial vision. But in a world where AI and hackathon-style events are a dime a dozen, it was important to differentiate. Everyone understood the assignment... and Buildathon was born.

But a live DJ playing tunes all day? Custom wrestling belts and jumble novelty checks? Ginormous cash prizes? A swag popup shop that ran only on an event-exclusive currency? A roaming camera crew like it was an NBA game? Skits involving free New York style pizza and energy drinks? A sunken garden water fountain installation?

What could possibly go wrong? 

But the results are undeniable. You put 300 of Airtable's most passionate builders together and what unfolds is some of the most focused, collaborative, high-energy, creative Airtable and AI solutioning I've ever seen. Hundreds of "bounties" were submitted, real apps for real use-cases, each with its own sophisticated, thoughtfully designed AI-powered workflow.

And despite the competitive spirit (the stakes were high, obv), the real magic was builders learning from each other, trading ideas, troubleshooting, and pushing each other’s builds further than they would have on their own. 

People who walked in as strangers were taking photo booth pics together by the end of the day. There was a sense of "omg I found my people". I mean, just search “Airtable Buildathon” on LinkedIn -- the energy speaks for itself. 

Allllll the credit goes to the team who made this real: Mikayla LaRosa, Madeline Johannsen, Grace Cheung, Meg Duffy, Paterson Wolfgram, Rachel McHugh, Christian Randell, Lindsey Puccio, Alex McDonnell, Victoria Plummer, Jonathan Katz, Bronwen Boyd, Caitlin Bishop, Claire Hartinger, Luis Pèrez, Yewon Kim, Calen Holbrooks, Anna Vander Broek, and a million more that character limits will prevent me from tagging.

And that's a wrap on another Gainsight #Pulse event 🫡

One of my favorite parts of events like these isn't the stage time. It's the homies. Catching up with friends I only see a few times a year, finally turning LinkedIn connects into IRL hangs, and spending a few days swapping notes, stories, and battle scars with folks who are all figuring this stuff out in real time. 

Also, the puppies (just don't tell Sully).

This year, the conversations (obv) seemed to orbit around AI and agents, AEO/GEO, MCP and headless platforms, and about 37 different predictions for what work will look like in six months. Equal parts exciting, fascinating... and slightly chaotic.

Also grateful for the opportunity to speak and share the Airtable Digital Programs story, "Making AI Work for You", to a room full of Customer Education and Community leaders. Three things I keep coming back to:

-- Intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. Connecting it to your real data and workflows is the actual work, and that work belongs to practitioners who live in those workflows every day.

-- Start with the right use case. The teams pulling ahead are the ones doing *more* AI, it's the ones doing the *right* AI: the workflow that repeats often, has a clear definition of done, and has a natural place for a human to check the work.

-- Prompts are becoming production agents. For our team, one content brief in Slack now fans out across a fleet of specialist agents, drafting course scripts, building demo Airtable environments, writing quiz items, and assembling elearning modules. Work that used to take a month lands in a morning.

Thanks to everyone who attended, connected, asked thoughtful questions, shared ideas, made the conversations memorable... and most important to those who flooded the session Q&A with DMB questions per my request 🤘

Always great to see folks like Erica Kuhl, Jon Wishart, Andrew Matsiavin, Eric Mistry, Kat Breeggemann, Sharon Castillo, Samantha Murray, Sonia Moaiery, Caroline Van Dyke, Matthew Nichols, Danny Pancratz, Amy Vujanich, Danielle Evans, Brian Oblinger... and to get the chance to unite the Community team together IRL Grace Cheung, Madeline Johannsen.

Noooo idea if there's an audience for this, but I spent ~$60 in AI credits the other day solving a problem for those DMB fans and concert poster collectors out there. 

Meet: DMB Poster Market ✨🎵

Important context: Dave Matthews Band commissions a unique poster for every single concert, the fans collect them, and they oftentimes sell out instantly and then trade on eBay for multiples on the retail price. If you've ever tried to track what your wall is worth, or what a missing one should cost you, you know it's a mess.

Built with Fable, DMB Poster Market catalogs every show from the last ten years, shows you that show's poster, and scrapes the resell data for that specific poster from eBay. Filter by year or by venue, mark your own posters to put a value on your collection, or add a poster to your watchlist to keep tabs on opportune times to buy if/when the market dips. 

Clicking into a show shows market trends, but you can also check out the poster listing on ExpressoBeans, revisit the show's setlist on DMBAlmanac, or dive right into the active listings on eBay.

posts.content:
Big news for Airtable builders and AI practitioners: we've launched the new Agentic Systems Design certification, available now in #AirtableAcademy.

For years, we've designed apps for the people using them. Clean schemas, engaging interfaces, the works. But now, it's not just people opening your base. It's AI agents. And they read your app very differently than humans do.

The next generation of builders will know how to design systems that agents can understand, navigate, and operate with confidence. So we built a certification for exactly that: Agentic Systems Design. 

It covers the stuff that *actually* makes agents work in Airtable. It focuses on the design decisions that determine whether an AI-powered workflow succeeds or falls apart in production. 

Things like:
↳ Designing schemas an agent can reliably read and understand
↳ Orchestrating multiple agents that hand off and collaborate cleanly 
↳ Knowing when to reach for Field Agents vs. automations vs. MCP 
↳ Building systems that don't fall over when an agent retries
↳ Creating review loops, guardrails, and recovery paths

If you're building in the agent era (you are... or you should be), come give it a shot. And for those that take & pass the exam, I can't wait to hear what you think (+ makes sure to tag us with #AirtableAcademy)!

Proud of the team that brought this one to life and excited to see it out in the world 🙌
